clue.text: Fashionable chap's a gossip who keeps a shop in a Dickens story

definitions.text: who keeps a shop in a Dickens story

parts.note: chic means stylish or fashionable
Ken is a typical man's name for a chap, with the 's giving the S
a talker is one who chatters or gossips

explanation.surface: A trendy fellow turns out to be a chatterbox running a shop in some Dickens tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Chickenstalker is the shopkeeper in Dickens's Christmas book The Chimes.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Chickenstalker is the shopkeeping character in Dickens's novella The Chimes.

clue.text: Criminal posed as moronic anarchist in London

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so the following letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A lawbreaker pretended to be a dimwitted bomb-thrower in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' rearranges POSED AS MORONIC. Comrade Ossipon is one of the anarchists in Conrad's London novel The Secret Agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Comrade Ossipon is a revolutionary figure among the plotters of Conrad's novel The Secret Agent, set in London.

clue.text: Popular Heller character is past legendary writer

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
Bruce Gold is the hero of Joseph Heller's novel Good as Gold
is contracts to 's, giving S
by can mean past, as in walking by

explanation.surface: A well-liked figure from a Joseph Heller novel has outlived a famous author.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Ingoldsby was the pen name of R. H. Barham, author of The Ingoldsby Legends, hence 'legendary'.
explanation.definitionFit: The pseudonymous Thomas Ingoldsby wrote the comic verse collection The Ingoldsby Legends.

clue.text: Kelvin performed tango — with unknown scrupulous writer?

parts.note: K is the symbol for the kelvin unit of temperature
ran can mean operated or performed, as a machine runs
T is tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet
z is a mathematical unknown, like x and y

explanation.surface: Someone called Kelvin danced a tango alongside a mysterious, conscientious author.
explanation.walkthrough: Judith Krantz wrote the bestseller Scruples, so the question-marked 'scrupulous writer' is a pun on her title.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Judith Krantz is best known for her bestseller titled Scruples.

clue.text: Word that's not even rarely seen in poetry

definitions.text: Word that's not even rarely seen in poetry

parts.words: Word that's not even rarely seen in poetry
parts.note: a contracted form of 'never' that turns up in verse; the joke is that far from being rare there, it appears in poems all the time

explanation.surface: A term that is in fact quite common in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: NE'ER is the poetic contraction of 'never', and 'not even rarely' is a playful way of saying 'never'.
explanation.definitionFit: This apostrophised contraction of never is a stock poeticism, and never can mean not even once.

clue.text: The priest included in written text in an old religious epic poem

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: included in means the priest's name goes inside the other piece

parts.note: hand means handwriting, the text a person writes
Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible

explanation.surface: A clergyman appears in a manuscript of an ancient sacred epic.
explanation.walkthrough: The Heliand is a ninth-century Old Saxon verse retelling of the Gospels.
explanation.definitionFit: This ninth-century Old Saxon work retells the Gospel story in alliterative verse.

clue.text: Probably in service, kind of bird on 197Os TV that's meeting duke

parts.note: The Liver Birds was a 1970s BBC sitcom about two young women in Liverpool
i.e., id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A servant in uniform, perhaps, a TV sitcom girl of the seventies meets an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: The Liver Birds was a British TV sitcom, named after the bird statues on Liverpool's Royal Liver Building. The clue prints '197Os' with a letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Servants such as footmen traditionally wear livery, so a uniformed person is likely a domestic employee.

clue.text: Something mistaken: fear of decapitation? Just the reverse

indicators.note: decapitation means cutting off the head, so the opening letter of the word for fear goes

parts.note: terror is extreme fear

explanation.surface: A mistaken idea: a dread of being beheaded? No, the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fear of decapitation' read 'just the reverse' becomes decapitation of fear: TERROR loses its head T.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake or blunder is something done wrongly, which is exactly what this word names.

clue.text: Dark hatred sets apart this member of a farming family

definitions.text: this member of a farming family

indicators.note: apart suggests the letters are broken up and set out afresh

explanation.surface: Grim loathing divides a member of a rural household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apart' rearranges DARK HATRED SETS. Seth Starkadder is the brooding son in Stella Gibbons's comic novel Cold Comfort Farm, where the family is famously full of dark feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Seth belongs to the Starkadders, the gloomy agricultural clan of Stella Gibbons's novel Cold Comfort Farm.

clue.text: Fallen angel made to follow Mary in the bible

definitions.text: to follow Mary in the bible

indicators.note: fallen suggests something tumbled down and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fallen angel was obliged to trail after the Virgin in scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible this name follows 'Mary' for one of Jesus's followers; 'Fallen' doubles as a nod to her traditional image as a reformed sinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Magdalene is a biblical follower of Jesus, so this surname comes after the given name Mary.

clue.text: A governess captivates this French author

indicators.note: captivates means holds captive, so the words a governess hold the name within them

explanation.surface: A nanny enthrals a writer from France.
explanation.walkthrough: Jules Verne was the French author of Around the World in Eighty Days.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne was a nineteenth-century novelist from France famed for adventure fiction.

clue.text: Cut out or remove (legally) about one line

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the legal word goes round the letter for line

parts.note: to abate a nuisance is to remove it in law
L stands for line, a single line

explanation.surface: An instruction to excise or legally strike out something concerning a single line of text.
explanation.walkthrough: To abate a nuisance is a legal term for ending or removing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons and scientists use this verb for removing tissue or material by cutting or erosion.

clue.text: Favourite writer — ultimately clever and playful poet

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as a teacher's pet

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word writer

parts.note: arch means slyly mischievous or knowingly playful

explanation.surface: A beloved author: in the end smart, roguish and a versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: Petrarch was the fourteenth-century Italian poet famed for his sonnets to Laura.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrarch was a celebrated Italian sonneteer of the fourteenth century.

clue.text: Detective's help improved keenness

parts.note: improved means better, as an improved version is a better one
edge means sharpness or keenness

explanation.surface: An investigator's assistant sharpened his skills.
explanation.walkthrough: Gabriel Betteredge is the house-steward who assists Sergeant Cuff in Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriel Betteredge is the steward who aids Sergeant Cuff's inquiries in Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone.

clue.text: This is plain sailing for a midshipman

definitions.meaning: plain sailing means simple and trouble-free
Mr Midshipman ... is Captain Marryat's naval novel and its hero

explanation.surface: Something straightforward for a junior naval officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plain sailing' looks nautical alongside 'midshipman', but it simply means straightforward.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain sailing means simple; Jack, hero of Marryat's novel Mr Midshipman Easy, bears the surname.

clue.text: Detective and poet who became a senior civil servant

definitions.text: who became a senior civil servant

parts.note: Lewis is the TV detective, Morse's sergeant who got his own series
T. S. Eliot was a modernist poet

explanation.surface: A police inspector and a versifier who rose high in Whitehall.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Eliot narrates C. P. Snow's Strangers and Brothers novels, rising from barrister to senior civil servant.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of C. P. Snow's Strangers and Brothers sequence ends up high in Whitehall's administration.

clue.text: Berlin author is joining this female club

parts.note: taken as written
her refers to a woman
a wood is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: A woman joins a club of her own in Berlin.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Isherwood wrote Goodbye to Berlin, the source of Cabaret.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Isherwood wrote Goodbye to Berlin and Mr Norris Changes Trains, set in the German capital.

clue.text: Line like this some bards use?

definitions.text: Line like this some bards use?

parts.words: Line like this some bards use?
parts.note: the clue itself scans with three stresses, LINE like THIS some BARDS use, so it names the verse measure it demonstrates

explanation.surface: A question about the kind of verse line poets employ.
explanation.definitionFit: This verse line has three metrical feet, and the clue itself scans with three stresses.

clue.text: Ephemeral text, like To the Lighthouse, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear signals that the words are to be said aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse is set on the Isle of Skye, so it is Skye writing

explanation.surface: A fleeting piece of writing, perhaps like a Virginia Woolf novel?
explanation.walkthrough: To the Lighthouse is set on the Hebridean island of Skye.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters traced in smoke by an aircraft drift and vanish within minutes.

clue.text: Written in futhorc, an important name in Germanic myth

definitions.text: an important name in Germanic myth

indicators.note: written in means the name appears inside the word that follows

explanation.surface: A great Norse god's name is inscribed in runes.
explanation.walkthrough: The futhorc is the Anglo-Saxon runic alphabet, named after its first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The thunder god of Norse and Germanic mythology bore this name.

clue.text: Reported source of disgrace for a marquess in London?

indicators.note: reported signals that a word is to be heard as spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: a stain is a mark of shame or dishonour

explanation.surface: An alleged scandal involving a titled aristocrat in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Steyne is the dissolute marquess in Thackeray's Vanity Fair, which is largely set in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's Vanity Fair features the Marquis of Steyne, a powerful and corrupt nobleman in London society.

clue.text: Moose in river that's flowing has gone west

indicators.note: flowing suggests the letters run loose into a new order

explanation.surface: An elk in a running river has drifted away westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's flowing' rearranges MOOSE IN plus R. 'Gone west' is slang for dead or finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Gone west is an idiom for dead or vanished, like the phrase meaning no longer exists.

clue.text: Boxer's utterance, perhaps sounding negative

indicators.note: sounding tells the solver to hear the word for negative rather than read it

parts.note: nay means no, a negative

explanation.surface: A fighter grunts something that sounds like a refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxer is the loyal carthorse in Orwell's Animal Farm, not a pugilist.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's cry is its whinny, so Orwell's horse Boxer would make this noise.

clue.text: Somewhere in Austria where saddlebacks might be found by a wet valley

parts.note: a saddleback is a British breed of pig, kept in a sty
a ria is a river valley drowned by the sea

explanation.surface: An Austrian region where saddle-shaped hills sit beside a rainy dale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saddlebacks' suggests ridged hills in an Alpine scene; here they are pigs (a black breed with a white band) in their pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Styria is a federal state of south-eastern Austria, capital Graz.

clue.text: Appreciate a rise of £1000 in one of two ways

indicators.note: in means the risen word sits inside the two symbols for a thousand pounds

parts.note: a grand, G, is slang for a thousand pounds
K, for kilo, also stands for a thousand pounds

indicators.note: in a down clue a rise means the word reads upwards, so its letters go backwards

parts.note: or links two alternatives, one of two ways

explanation.surface: Welcome a thousand-pound pay increase in either of two forms.
explanation.walkthrough: A thousand pounds can be written two ways, as a grand or as K for kilo, so the clue's one '£1000' supplies both outer letters; in a down clue 'a rise of' reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: This science-fiction coinage means to understand intuitively and deeply.

clue.text: Non-standard burlesque artist or poet

indicators.note: non-standard means without the standard, so the golf word for the standard score is dropped

parts.note: a parodist writes burlesques, mocking imitations

explanation.surface: An unconventional stripper or versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-standard' looks like an anagram signal but means 'lacking par', par being the standard score in golf; take PAR from PARODIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An odist is a writer of odes, hence a lyric versifier.

clue.text: This is obscene, and it's something disliked, even with a different ending

definitions.text: This is obscene, and it's something disliked, even with a different ending

parts.words: This is obscene, and it's something disliked, even with a different ending
parts.note: a smutty term is the literal reading; figuratively the phrase means an idea people shun, and swapping its final letter gives a phrase for unpleasant tasks

explanation.surface: Something both lewd and unpopular, whichever way it ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Literally a rude word; figuratively something people hate to mention. Change the last letter and DIRTY WORK is also disliked.
explanation.definitionFit: An obscene term is rude language, and figuratively the phrase means a notion people dislike.

clue.text: Independent northern lady needing to avoid dodgy dealer acquiring farmland

indicators.note: acquiring means the first pieces take in the farmland word

parts.note: to shirk is to avoid a duty

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable, so the letters of dealer are reshuffled

parts.note: a ley is arable land temporarily under grass

explanation.surface: A self-reliant woman from the north must steer clear of a crooked trader buying up fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' rearranges DEALER into EELDAR; SHIRK plus EELDAR acquires LEY. Shirley Keeldar is the spirited Yorkshire heiress in Charlotte Brontë's Shirley.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirley Keeldar is the spirited heiress of Charlotte Brontë's Yorkshire novel Shirley.
